note: Reference data only. Phone NFC reads 13.56 MHz (ISO 14443 / 15693 / 18092). 125 kHz credentials are listed for identification, they cannot be read by a phone.

cards.name: MIFARE Classic 1K
cards.notes: Clonable with a phone in seconds. Still used by hotels, gyms, older offices and some transit systems.

cards.name: MIFARE Classic 4K
cards.notes: Same weakness as 1K. Sectors 0-31 are 4 blocks, 32-39 are 16 blocks.

cards.name: MIFARE Ultralight
cards.notes: Event tickets, single-use passes. No cryptographic protection.

cards.name: MIFARE Ultralight C
cards.notes: Adds 3DES mutual authentication. Legacy 3DES is considered weak today.

cards.name: NTAG213
cards.notes: The most common sticker tag. NDEF URL/ text payloads.

cards.name: NTAG215
cards.notes: Amiibo-compatible size. Common in access-control stickers.

cards.name: NTAG216
cards.notes: Largest NTAG. Often used for vCard and Wi-Fi sharing tags.

cards.name: MIFARE DESFire EV1
cards.notes: Solid when AES is used. Legacy DES mode is the weak point.

cards.name: MIFARE DESFire EV2
cards.notes: Adds transaction MAC and proximity verification against relay attacks.

cards.name: MIFARE DESFire EV3
cards.notes: Current generation for corporate badges and campus cards.

cards.name: MIFARE Plus
cards.notes: Drop-in Crypto1 replacement. Once switched to SL3 it is not clonable.

cards.name: ICODE SLIX (ISO 15693)
cards.notes: Longer read range (up to ~1 m). Library books, laundry tags, industrial asset labels.

cards.name: FeliCa
cards.notes: Japan / Hong Kong transit and payment. Many phones can read it but not emulate it.

cards.name: Calypso
cards.notes: Transit standard in France, Belgium, Portugal, Brazil, Egypt and others.

cards.name: Visa contactless
cards.notes: PAN and expiry are readable without authentication; the cryptogram is not replayable.

cards.name: Mastercard contactless
cards.notes: Same EMV flow as Visa, different AID and application template.

cards.name: American Express contactless
cards.notes: Amex Pay / ExpressPay application.

cards.name: UnionPay QuickPass
cards.notes: China mainland debit/credit contactless.

cards.name: JCB contactless
cards.notes: Japan-issued cards, also accepted across Asia.

cards.name: MIR contactless
cards.notes: Russian domestic payment scheme.

cards.name: HID iCLASS / iCLASS SE
cards.notes: Corporate badges. Legacy iCLASS (non-SE) keys have been recovered publicly, SE is not affected.

cards.name: HID Seos
cards.notes: Not clonable with a phone. Often paired with iCLASS for migration.

cards.name: LEGIC advant
cards.notes: Common in European building access and time clocks.

cards.name: HID Prox (125 kHz)
cards.notes: Older office fobs. NOT readable by a phone: needs a 125 kHz coil (Flipper Zero, Proxmark).

cards.name: EM4100 / EM4102 (125 kHz)
cards.notes: Trivially clonable with cheap hardware, but again: not via phone NFC.

cards.name: China City Union card (住建部)
cards.security: Mixed — legacy Crypto1 in older issues
cards.notes: Older city bus cards are MIFARE Classic inside. Newer issues moved to CPU cards.

cards.name: China T-Union (交通联合)
cards.notes: National intercity transit card. Modern issues are not clonable.

cards.name: Troika / social cards
cards.notes: Representative of modern transit migrations: MIFARE Classic → Plus/DESFire.

cards.name: Hotel room key (RFID)
cards.notes: Many chains still ship MIFARE Classic with per-hotel keys. Check the SAK before assuming.

cards.name: NFC Forum Type 1
cards.notes: Rare today. Read/write with NDEF.

cards.name: NFC Forum Type 3
cards.notes: FeliCa-based tags used in Japan.

cards.name: NFC Forum Type 4
cards.notes: Smart posters, ticketing, passports' contactless interface.

cards.name: ePassport (ICAO 9303)
cards.notes: Readable only with the MRZ key printed inside the document. Not a cloning target.

cards.name: NFC ring / implant
cards.notes: Usually just an NTAG213 in resin — behaves exactly like a sticker.

cards.name: amiibo
cards.notes: NTAG215 with a locked data page. Can be cloned to a blank NTAG215.

cards.name: Tesla key card
cards.notes: Unlocked by the car, not by the card. Cloning the UID alone does nothing.

cards.name: DESFire transit ticket
cards.notes: Typical for new deployments in Europe and Asia.

cards.name: MIFARE Classic Mini
cards.notes: Smallest Classic variant. Same weaknesses as 1K, only 5 sectors so hotels and gyms use it for day passes.

cards.name: MIFARE Ultralight EV1
cards.security: No crypto on MF0UL11; 3DES on MF0UL21
cards.notes: Transit single-ride tickets, event wristbands, disposable passes. UID is readable by any phone.

cards.name: NTAG I2C plus
cards.notes: NFC tag wired to a microcontroller — toys, appliances, smart posters. Tapping it can trigger hardware.

cards.name: NTAG 424 DNA
cards.notes: Anti-counterfeit tag: every read returns a signed, changing URL. Used on luxury goods and tax stamps. Not clonable.

cards.name: MIFARE DESFire Light
cards.notes: Entry-level secure element, sold as a cheaper EV2. Used for campus cards and small access systems.

cards.name: MIFARE Plus S (SL1)
cards.security: Crypto1 in SL1, AES in SL2/SL3
cards.notes: Ships in Security Level 1 so it looks exactly like a Classic card. If the deployment never upgraded it, it still clones.

cards.name: MIFARE Plus X
cards.notes: Usually deployed at SL3: the reader authenticates with AES and the card refuses Classic commands.

cards.name: ICODE SLIX2
cards.notes: Longer read range than 14443 (up to ~1 m with a big antenna). Library books, medical trays, industrial bins.

cards.name: Tag-it HF-I
cards.notes: Bare memory with no protection at all. Still found in laundry and garment tracking.

cards.name: FeliCa Lite-S
cards.notes: Sony's system, dominant in Japan. 212 kbit/s, 10 ms transaction — that is why it is used for transit gates.

cards.name: Cartes Bancaires (CB)
cards.notes: French domestic scheme. Even with the card data read, a payment needs a fresh cryptogram generated by the chip's secret key. Copying it to a phone does not work.

cards.name: Girocard (Germany)
cards.notes: German debit scheme. Contactless limit and CVM rules are enforced by the terminal, not the card.

cards.name: Discover / Diners
cards.notes: US scheme, also issued in Japan as Diners. Same EMV protection.

cards.name: Bancontact
cards.notes: Belgian debit scheme, run by Worldline.

cards.name: Elo
cards.notes: Brazilian scheme, co-badged with Visa/Mastercard abroad.

cards.name: RuPay
cards.notes: Indian domestic scheme by NPCI.

cards.name: Troy
cards.notes: Turkish domestic scheme.

cards.name: Apple Pay (DPAN)
cards.notes: The phone never holds your real card number: the bank issues a separate DPAN and each payment is signed inside the SE. There is nothing to copy out.

cards.name: Google Pay (DPAN)
cards.notes: Same tokenisation model as Apple Pay, hosted by the bank or by Google.

cards.name: Samsung Pay (MST + NFC)
cards.notes: The only phone that also emulates a magnetic stripe (MST) so it works on old terminals. That is a Samsung hardware feature, not something an app can reproduce.

cards.name: Navigo (Île-de-France)
cards.notes: Paris transit pass. Calypso stores the contract in secure sectors; the pass is validated against a signed counter, so a copy fails at the gate.

cards.name: Oyster (London)
cards.notes: TfL migrated off Classic years ago precisely because Classic was clonable. Balance lives server-side.

cards.name: Octopus (Hong Kong)
cards.notes: Hong Kong, China. One of the oldest and most copied closed-loop purses.

cards.name: Suica / PASMO (Japan)
cards.notes: Japan. FeliCa is also what the phone's own NFC-F mode talks to.

cards.name: Clipper (Bay Area)
cards.notes: San Francisco Bay Area. Value stored in a secure file, not a plain block.

cards.name: T-money (Korea)
cards.notes: Seoul metropolitan area.

cards.name: EZ-Link (Singapore)
cards.notes: Singapore stored-value card.

cards.name: Opal (Sydney)
cards.notes: New South Wales.

cards.name: myki (Victoria)
cards.notes: Melbourne.

cards.name: Troika (Moscow)
cards.notes: Moscow. Older Troika cards were Classic-based, which is why the transport authority replaced them.

cards.name: Charlie (Boston)
cards.notes: MBTA. Classic-based, so the classic attacks apply — which is exactly why it was retired.

cards.name: OMNY (New York)
cards.notes: New York replaced MetroCard with open-loop EMV: your own bank card is the ticket, no stored value.

cards.name: HID iCLASS SE
cards.notes: Corporate badges. The SIO is signed; a raw UID clone is rejected by SE readers.

cards.name: Indala (Motorola)
cards.notes: Legacy 125 kHz badge. Trivially clonable with a T5577 — which is why most sites replaced it.

cards.name: AWID
cards.notes: US access control brand, 125 kHz, no crypto.

cards.name: Paradox
cards.notes: Alarm and access systems, common in Canada and Europe.

cards.name: NEDAP
cards.notes: Dutch brand, vehicle access and time clocks.

cards.name: Salto (MIFARE)
cards.security: MIFARE Classic or DESFire depending on generation
cards.notes: Hotel and campus locks. Older Salto installations are Classic-based.

cards.name: Onity
cards.notes: Hotel locks. The 2012 magstripe encoder flaw is the textbook case of a physical-access vulnerability.

cards.name: VingCard / ASSA ABLOY
cards.notes: Hotel locks. Modern generations use DESFire with mutual authentication.

cards.name: T5577 (clone chip)
cards.notes: The blank chip everyone uses to copy EM4100/HID Prox badges. Read-write, no protection.

cards.name: Hitag 2
cards.notes: Car immobilisers and older access systems. The cipher has been broken publicly since 2007.

cards.name: Hitag S
cards.notes: Harder than Hitag 2 but still analysed. Used in vehicle keys and industrial tags.

cards.name: ISO 11784/11785 microchip
cards.notes: Pet and livestock implants. Fully readable with the right coil; the UID is the whole payload.

cards.name: German eID (nPA)
cards.notes: Contactless national ID. PACE derives a session key from a 6-digit PIN, so a passive read gives you nothing.

cards.name: Estonian eID
cards.notes: Contactless capable since the 2018 generation.

cards.name: Carte Vitale (France)
cards.notes: French health card. Contact-only for the patient version; the professional version (CPF) has a contactless interface.

cards.name: CNIe (France, 2021+)
cards.security: PACE, BAC for the eMRTD applet
cards.notes: New French ID card. The contactless chip holds the same data as the passport chip.

cards.name: Skylanders portal tag
cards.notes: Toy-to-life figures. The figure's ID is a plain block — that is why emulator apps exist.

cards.name: LEGO Dimensions tag
cards.notes: Same idea as Skylanders, NTAG-based.

cards.name: EV charging RFID
cards.notes: Charging subscriptions are often a bare UID — which is why some networks moved to app-based auth.

cards.name: Gym / leisure wristband
cards.notes: Wristbands at pools and festivals are frequently Classic with a default key.

cards.name: NFC Forum Type 5 tag
cards.notes: Long-range sticker tags. Type 5 is the 15693 flavour of the NFC Forum taxonomy.
